role: Manager with budget or people responsibility
suspicion_text: Maybe whether we go by the system or by what our own team on the ground is saying.
Q1_text: Mostly I am on two reports. The daily sales and stock report which comes on Power BI, and the option performance report for my category which I open before every Monday review. The first thing I look at is the sell through percentage for the new season options, and after that the stock cover by store. If sell through is looking fine I do not go further, which I know is a bad habit.
Q2_text: Two weeks back I had to decide the repeat order for one printed kurta option. The report showed sell through at 62 per cent in four weeks, which is good for us, and it was marked green for repeat. What I noticed was that the sale was coming almost fully from three stores and the rest were flat, so I asked my planner for the store wise split and I also called the Bengaluru cluster manager. He said those three stores had put the option on the front table because of a display change, not because customers were asking for it. Finally I placed a repeat but for half the quantity, and only for those clusters.
Q3_text: Honestly, only by looking at whether the numbers are moving. If yesterday's sale is showing zero for some stores at ten in the morning, then I know the sync has not happened. Our report does not show any warning at all. There is a refreshed time at the bottom in small letters and nobody looks at it. What makes me doubt is when a number is too good, because in retail we usually know which options are working before the report tells us.
Q4_text: Yes. In March the report was showing one particular store as our top performer for two weeks, and I could not believe it because that store is in a small market and it has never come in the top ten. When I asked, it came out that a bulk institutional order had been billed from that store for some tax reason at the head office end. So the sale was real but it was not that store's sale, and my whole planning for that cluster would have gone wrong.
Q5_text: I raised it with my planning head and with finance on mail. Finance said it is a billing decision and it will not be changed. Nobody put any note in the report or anywhere else, so that store is still sitting in the ranking for that month. What changed is only my own behaviour, I check the top movers myself before planning a repeat. So I adjusted, the system stayed as it is.
Q6_text: A report carries more weight, no doubt about it. If I say an option will not work because I have seen the fabric and the fit trials, that is treated as my feeling. If I show the sell through screen, the discussion finishes there itself. Last season I stopped a big buy because our store staff were reporting fit complaints, and I was asked three times to justify it, till the returns data came and proved the same point.
Q7_text: They are not equal. If I buy on the basis of the report and the option fails, then it is a market issue and everybody says the season was bad. If I have gone against the report and it fails, then it becomes my buying decision and it stays in people's memory. My senior will not say anything openly, but at the year end review it comes back.
Q8_text: One of our store managers in Mysuru kept telling me that the size ratio we were sending was wrong, that the smaller sizes were sitting and the larger ones were finishing in a week. He raised it on the store managers call for almost two months. Nobody wrote it anywhere and the allocation logic did not change. It got corrected only when the head of retail visited that store and saw the empty pegs himself.
Q9_text: Yes it does. We end up discussing price, discount and quantity, because those are the three things the report has columns for. What we never discuss is whether the option itself is wrong for that market, or whether the store staff need product training, because there is no number to show for it. So the conversation becomes how much discount to give, when the real answer may be that we should not have bought that option at all.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about choosing where to open the next store the dashboard indicated that the site scored 87 and should be opened next quarter, while what you knew locally was that the footfall counter at that site had been offline for 47 days. You chose: Recommend Tiruppur for Q3, as the Site Score indicates.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: If I am honest, the score is what I can defend. Sitting in a review, if I say the site score is 87 and the system said open, nobody will question me much. If I say my area officer feels the crowd is only bus stand traffic, the first question will be what is your data. In real life I would still go with the score for the recommendation, but I would ask her to send that observation on mail so that it is recorded somewhere. That mail is the only protection we have if it goes wrong later.
Q11_text: The screen should show, next to each number, when that data last came in. Not in small letters at the bottom, but next to the number itself and in red if it is old. Right now there is no way for me to know that a counter is dead, and I cannot argue about something I cannot see. The second thing is that a person who raises a doubt should get a written reply within a week, otherwise people simply stop raising.
Q12_text: Only that we are always deciding in a hurry. The buy has to be closed by a date and the report is the fastest thing available, so even when we have a doubt we go ahead, because checking takes two weeks and we do not have two weeks. I think speed is a bigger reason than trust.
outcome: Billing practice was not changed and the store stayed in the ranking; she now checks the top movers by hand before planning any repeat
codes: no_refresh_warning; billing_artefact_in_sales_data; verbal_objection_only; defensibility_of_reports; blame_asymmetry; option_narrowing; time_pressure

suspicion_text: Something about how much people trust the dashboard when it goes against what they are hearing from customers.
Q1_text: I am basically living inside two screens. Our customer health dashboard which I open first thing, and the ticket dashboard in the afternoon. The first thing I look at is the red accounts list and the health score movement since last week. If nothing has turned red I move on to my calls.
Q2_text: Last month I had to decide which accounts go into the quarterly business review list. The dashboard gives a churn risk score and I took the top eight red accounts from it. I checked the ticket count and the login trend for those accounts and both were matching, so I built the list straight from the screen. Later my manager pointed out that two of our biggest accounts were sitting in green and had not logged in for three weeks, which the score had not picked up because their usage is seasonal. So my list was technically correct and practically wrong.
Q3_text: There is a last synced time on the top right and I do check it, but to be honest if it says synced I assume everything inside is fine. The tool shows a banner when the sync fails completely. If only one event type stops coming there is nothing shown and the score just drifts. I learnt this the hard way when our mobile app events stopped flowing and half our accounts suddenly started looking healthier.
Q4_text: Yes, that same mobile events case. The dashboard was showing engagement going up for a set of accounts in a week when we had actually had an outage, which made no sense at all. I checked with the data team and they said a tracking key had been changed in a release, so the app events were going to a different property. Around three weeks of data was affected before anybody noticed.
Q5_text: I put it in the engineering channel and tagged the analytics owner. He fixed it in a few days and confirmed on the thread. Nothing was written anywhere else, and the health scores for those three weeks were never recalculated, so if you pull that period today it still shows the wrong picture. Nobody raised it again because by then we had moved on to the next quarter.
Q6_text: A number wins, always. In our reviews if you say an account is at risk, the first question is what does the health score say. If the score is green and you are saying red, then you have to bring evidence like mails from the customer. It becomes easier to just wait for the score to turn red, which is a bad way to work but that is what actually happens.
Q7_text: If I follow the dashboard and we lose the account, then it becomes a product issue or a model issue, and there is a whole discussion on improving the score. If I go against it, spend two weeks on an account that the score said was healthy, and it still churns, then it looks like I wasted my time on the wrong account. So there is definitely more risk in going against it, especially at my level.
Q8_text: Our support lead kept saying that the ticket sentiment tagging was wrong, that angry customers were getting tagged as neutral because the tagging is automatic. She said it in standups many times. It was not written anywhere, there is no place to write such things with us. It got picked up only when a customer escalated to our CEO and somebody went back and actually read the tickets.
Q9_text: Definitely. We only talk about what is on the dashboard, which is usage, tickets and renewal date. Whether the customer's champion has left the company, or whether their own business is going down, never appears on the screen and so it never comes up in the weekly review. Those two things are what actually kill accounts.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about moving specialists off customer retention the dashboard indicated that only six accounts were at risk and three specialists could be reassigned, while what you knew locally was that an account manager said two of the largest customers had gone quiet. You chose: Move the three specialists to onboarding, as the dashboard recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I chose to move the specialists because the dashboard was showing risk down and utilisation at 34 per cent, and honestly that is the exact situation where my leadership would ask why three people are sitting idle. In my company the pressure is to show that the team is being used efficiently, and one account manager's comment would not be enough to hold them back. Thinking about it now, the part I missed is that a quiet account and a healthy account look exactly the same on a usage screen, and I know this from my own experience also.
Q11_text: The tool should show a freshness indicator per source, and it should flag when an account has gone silent instead of showing it green. Silence is not health. On the culture side, my manager should ask me what I am seeing and not only what the score is saying, because right now the meeting starts from the dashboard and anything which is not on it has to fight to get in.
Q12_text: One thing. We are all fairly young in this function and nobody has taught us how a health score is actually calculated. I have never seen the logic. So when it says 82 I have no way of knowing whether that is meaningful or not, I simply take it as a fact.
outcome: Tracking key fixed within a few days but the three affected weeks of health scores were never recalculated
codes: partial_feed_failure; silent_accounts_look_healthy; chat_only_objection; score_logic_opaque; utilisation_pressure; blame_asymmetry; declining_engagement_across_vignettes

role: Manager with budget or people responsibility
seniority: Senior manager or head of function
suspicion_text: I think it is about whether we follow the system or our own judgement when the two are not matching.
level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: In a week I am opening the bed occupancy and discharge dashboard almost every day, and the operation theatre utilisation report twice a week. The first thing I see is the occupancy percentage ward wise and the number of discharges still pending after twelve noon, because that decides whether we can accept evening admissions. After that I look at the nursing ratio for the night shift.
Q2_text: Last month we had to decide whether to open the second floor ward for elective cases, because the dashboard was showing occupancy at 71 per cent for three weeks together. Before deciding I asked the nursing superintendent to give me the actual bed status at eight in the evening for one full week, not the midnight census which the system takes. The evening figures were much higher, close to 88 per cent, because most discharges were happening after four and the beds were only free at night. We did not open the ward, we worked on the discharge summary process instead. The dashboard was not wrong, it was measuring at the hour when the hospital looks emptiest.
Q3_text: In our hospital information system the data comes from what the ward clerk enters, so it is only as current as the entry. If a nurse is handling an emergency, the discharge entry may happen two hours later, and the dashboard will show a bed as occupied when it is actually free and cleaned. The system does show a warning if the interface with the lab is down, but for delayed entry there is nothing at all. So before any staffing decision I cross check against the ward round list, because for us a wrong number is a patient safety issue and not only a cost issue.
Q4_text: Yes, last quarter the dashboard was showing the average length of stay coming down nicely for the medical ward. I did not believe it because the ward was full and the same patients were there when I did my rounds. On checking, we found that patients being transferred to the ICU were getting counted as discharges, so their stay was being closed and a fresh admission created. One patient was becoming two short stays.
Q5_text: I raised it in the monthly quality meeting, and with us every quality meeting has minutes and an action owner, so it was written down the same day. The IT team took about six weeks but they corrected the logic and also gave us a revised trend for the previous two quarters. In this case the system worked. I would say it worked because it went into the quality forum. If I had only told IT informally it would still be pending.
Q6_text: In a clinical setting the documentation carries the weight. If a decision is questioned in an incident review, the first question is what was recorded at that time. A report is stronger than an opinion, but a nursing note is also treated as a record with us, so the gap is not as wide as it may be in a corporate setup. Still, if I stop a rota change because I feel the ward is not safe, I am expected to write down why, whereas if I follow the rota system nobody asks me anything.
Q7_text: They are not the same, but in our case it is the opposite of what you may be expecting. If I follow the system, reduce the staff, and something happens to a patient, then it is my responsibility, because the final rota is signed by me and not by the software. If I overrule the system and keep extra staff, the worst that happens is a question from finance about the agency cost. So the safer side for me is to keep the nurse, and that is why I do not cut staffing on the basis of a prediction.
Q8_text: Our ward sister told us for many weeks that the fall risk score was not reflecting correctly for the elderly patients, because the score was being entered at admission and never updated after that. She raised it with the nursing head and it went into the quality register. It took time but it was answered, and now the score has to be reviewed every shift. I will be fair and say this happens with us because of the accreditation audits. An open entry in the register becomes a finding, so somebody has to close it.
Q9_text: It does narrow it. When the rota tool gives an option, we discuss numbers of staff and nothing else, because the tool counts heads and not experience. Two junior nurses are not equal to one senior nurse at night, and the screen has no way of showing that. Keeping a float nurse for the floor is another option which appears nowhere, so it comes up only if some person in the meeting remembers to raise it.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about renewing a supplier at increased volume the dashboard indicated that the supplier scored 98.6 per cent and should be renewed at higher volume, while what you knew locally was that the inspector had been passing batches by eye because the test rig was out of calibration. You chose: Renew at increased volume, as the scorecard recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: In that one I went with the scorecard, and thinking about it now, it is because supplier quality is not my subject. In my own ward I will question a number immediately, but in somebody else's area I assume that the person who built the score knows what he is doing. That is the honest answer. If it were a medical consumable in my hospital I would have called the inspector first, because 98.6 per cent with zero defect reports is not a real number, nothing is that clean.
Q11_text: One change in the tool, it must show when the last entry came from each source. The bigger one is cultural. The person raising the doubt should not be the one who has to prove it. Today if I say a number looks wrong, the burden comes on me to produce evidence while the report is assumed correct until I disprove it. If it were the other way round, people would speak up much more often.
Q12_text: Only one point. In hospitals the people who know the truth are the nurses and the ward clerks, and they are the ones with no access to the dashboard at all. They enter the data and they never see the report that is made from it. If they could see it, half of these errors would get caught on the same day.
outcome: Length of stay logic corrected in about six weeks and the previous two quarters were restated
codes: delayed_data_entry; transfer_counted_as_discharge; formal_quality_register; objection_answered; safety_asymmetry_favours_caution; skill_mix_invisible; data_entrants_cannot_see_report

role: Manager with budget or people responsibility
seniority: Senior manager or head of function
suspicion_text: Whether people accept what the system says even when their own staff are telling them something different.
level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: I am not a dashboard person as such, but there are two things I have to see every week. The incoming inspection summary from SAP and the customer complaint tracker which our quality engineer maintains. The first thing I look at is the rejection PPM for the week and after that the open corrective action list. I will be frank, I trust the corrective action list more, because a person is updating it and he has to answer for it in the meeting.
Q2_text: Recently we had to decide whether to move one supplier from sampling inspection to hundred per cent. The SAP report was showing his rejection PPM coming down from 1800 to about 400 over two quarters, which looks like a good improvement. Before deciding I checked how many of his lots were actually inspected in that period. It turned out most of his lots were coming in as direct to line under a deviation that production had taken during the volume ramp up. So the PPM was low because we had stopped checking, not because he had improved. We continued hundred per cent inspection and closed that deviation.
Q3_text: For me the test is simple. I ask when was the last calibration and who has signed the entry. If a gauge is not calibrated then whatever the system shows is only a number, it is not a measurement. Our SAP does not warn about any of this, it will happily accept a reading from an instrument whose validity expired last year. That is why the internal audit checks the calibration register separately, and I have myself held back the clearance of a lot because the plug gauge was out of validity.
Q4_text: Many times, but the one I remember is the leak test machine. The report was showing hundred per cent pass for two days continuously, which in a leak test is not possible, some leakage always comes. I went to the shop floor and found that the fixture clamp had worn out, so the fixture was sitting slightly open and the machine was reading atmosphere as a pass. The operator was not doing anything wrong, he simply had no reason to doubt a machine that was showing pass.
Q5_text: I stopped the dispatch the same day and raised a quality alert, which in our system has a number and goes straight to the plant head. Maintenance replaced the clamp within two days and we quarantined the entire lot of that shift. It is recorded and it came up in the management review also. In our line of work if you do not record it and the part reaches the customer, then you are personally answerable, so everybody records.
Q6_text: In quality, evidence means traceability. If I can show the inspection record, the batch number and the calibration certificate, then my position is strong. A report by itself is not enough with us, because the auditor will ask where the report came from. Having said that, in the commercial meetings a report does carry more weight than my opinion, and I have seen purchase decisions taken on a supplier scorecard which I would never have taken.
Q7_text: For me the two are equal, and I will tell you why. If a defective part reaches the customer, the question asked is why did quality release it, not what did the system say. The system is not signing the release note, I am signing it. So I cannot take shelter behind a report. In other departments it may be different, in quality the signature is personal and everybody knows it.
Q8_text: Our line inspector told us for almost a month that the hardness values from one testing machine were drifting, because the same sample was giving different values on different shifts. The first reaction from the team was that he is not doing the test properly. He is a diploma holder with twenty years on that machine, so I asked him to record ten readings a day for one week and bring it to me. On paper it was very clear and the machine went for servicing. My learning is that he was right from day one and we made him prove it, which is not correct.
Q9_text: Yes, when we sit with a supplier scorecard the discussion becomes only about score and volume. The option of going and doing a process audit at his plant does not come on the table, because it costs travel and it has no number attached to it. Same with training his operators. These are the things that actually fix quality and they never come up in a review, because the scorecard has no column for them.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about filing a price increase the dashboard indicated that every tracked competitor sat above you and a 7 per cent rise was safe, while what you knew locally was that your sales head had photographed a rival selling below you on promotion. You chose: Hold the increase until the competitor price capture is re-run and checked against store visits.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: Pricing is not my area, but the principle is the same as calibration. If the capture job has not run for three weeks then the price on that screen is not today's price, it is last month's price, and taking a full quarter's decision on it is not correct. What would drive my choice is that the sales head has physically seen the rival's price in the store. A photograph from the field beats a crawl that nobody has checked. In my experience the man standing in front of the machine, or in this case in front of the shelf, is usually right.
Q11_text: Two things and both are small. Every report should carry the date of the last successful data load printed on the report itself, exactly the way a calibration sticker is stuck on an instrument. And there should be a place to enter a doubt against a number, with a person who has to close it, like our corrective action system. If quality can run this discipline for parts, the same discipline can be run for data.
Q12_text: One thing I want to say. In our plants the data comes from people who are already overloaded. The operator is entering a reading between two cycles, and if you keep adding entries he will start writing the previous value. So when a report looks too steady, that steadiness itself is the warning sign. Nobody teaches this to the people who design these dashboards.
outcome: Dispatch stopped the same day, worn clamp replaced within two days and the whole shift lot quarantined
codes: uncalibrated_gauge; deviation_hides_rejections; formal_quality_alert; personal_signature_accountability; ground_staff_made_to_prove_it; scorecard_excludes_process_audit; data_entry_burden

suspicion_text: I think you wanted to see if the warning on the dashboard changes the decision or not.
Q1_text: During the admission season I am on the counselling dashboard the whole day, and I also see the fee collection report every evening. The first thing I look at is the number of applications received against yesterday, and the conversion from application to fee paid. In the off season it comes down to maybe twice a week.
Q2_text: In June we had to decide whether to increase the counsellor allocation for one programme, because the dashboard was showing enquiry to application conversion at only 18 per cent for that programme against 30 for the others. Before recommending anything I pulled the call logs for a week and I also sat with two counsellors. It came out that most enquiries for that programme were coming from a lead campaign in a state where we have no hostel capacity, so students were dropping off the moment they asked about accommodation. Adding counsellors would have solved nothing. We changed the campaign targeting instead.
Q3_text: The CRM shows a last updated time, and I have learnt to check whether today's leads are appearing at all. If the count is unusually round, or exactly the same as yesterday, then something is wrong. There is no warning as such, it will simply show the last available data. Once the lead feed from one portal stopped for four days and the dashboard just showed lower enquiries, and we all thought our campaign was underperforming.
Q4_text: Yes, that same case. The report was showing our enquiries dropping around 30 per cent in a week and everybody assumed the campaign was failing. I did not believe it because our counsellors were saying their calling lists were full and they were not able to finish the follow ups. When we checked, the interface from one lead portal had stopped after they changed something at their end, so those leads were sitting there and not coming into the CRM at all.
Q5_text: I told our IT coordinator and I also mentioned it in the daily admissions meeting. It was fixed in about a week once the portal responded. Nobody wrote it down anywhere, and the weekly report which had already gone to the Dean showed the drop without any note against it. In the next meeting it was again referred to as a dip in enquiries. I did clarify verbally but by then the discussion had moved on.
Q6_text: A report is definitely easier to defend. If the dashboard says conversion is low, then that is accepted as a fact. If I say the leads themselves are of poor quality, then I am expected to prove it with numbers, and compiling that takes two or three days. In one review I was told that unless I can show it in the data it is only a perception.
Q7_text: They are not the same. If I follow the dashboard and the admission target is not met, then it becomes a market issue or a campaign issue and it is shared by everybody. If I do something different, like stopping a campaign on my own reading, and the numbers fall, then it is my call and it will be pointed out. So people prefer to keep following the report and let the season decide.
Q8_text: Our senior counsellor kept saying that the lead score in the CRM was not reliable, because students who were only comparing colleges were coming as hot leads simply for filling the form completely. She raised it with the marketing team a few times. There is no formal place to record such a thing with us, so it stayed as a discussion. It has still not changed.
Q9_text: Yes. The dashboard gives us conversion, source and counsellor performance, so every discussion becomes about calling more, calling faster, or changing the counsellor. Things like the programme content, or the hostel and scholarship issue which is the real reason students drop out of the funnel, do not appear on any screen, so they do not come up in the review at all.
Q10_prompt: In the study you have just completed, in the scenario about filing a price increase the dashboard indicated that every tracked competitor sat above you and a 7 per cent rise was safe, while what you knew locally was that your sales head had photographed a rival selling below you on promotion. You chose: File the 7 per cent increase, as the pricing engine recommends.Looking back, what would drive your choice if this were a real decision at your work?
Q10_text: I filed the increase because the engine was showing every competitor above us, and my own reading of the market is not part of that system. In our case also, fee decisions are taken on a comparison sheet of competitor fees, and if the sheet says we are below then increasing is the obvious recommendation. Looking back, the mistake is that a photograph from the field is newer information than a crawl which ran three weeks ago, and I did not weigh it properly. In real life I think I would have called two or three stores myself before filing, because once it is filed it cannot be changed for the whole quarter.
Q11_text: If the dashboard itself showed which sources have not sent data today, I would catch these things on the same morning instead of after two weeks. And there should be a simple comment box against any number where I can record a doubt, which the reporting team has to close. As of now the doubt lives in my head and in one WhatsApp message.
Q12_text: Only that in our sector the season is very short, around three months, and by the time a data problem is found the admissions are over. A mistake in the dashboard in June cannot be corrected in September, the year is gone. That urgency is completely missing when people design these reports.
outcome: Lead feed restored in about a week, but the weekly report showing the drop was never annotated and the drop was discussed again as a demand dip

seniority: Senior manager or head of function
suspicion_text: You are checking whether the warning on the screen makes any difference to what people decide.
level: Senior manager or head of function
Q1_text: I open the outage dashboard first thing in the morning and again in the evening, and the SCADA summary is anyway running on the screen in the control room. The first thing I look at is the number of feeders out and the duration, and then the distribution transformer failure count for the day. In our business the first question from the customer and from the regulator is about interruptions, so I have to know that number before anybody asks me.
Q2_text: Two months back we had to decide whether to defer the maintenance of one 33 kV feeder to after the monsoon. The reliability report was showing that feeder with zero tripping for four months, which normally means it is healthy. What I checked was the load pattern and the last thermography report, and the thermography showed a hot spot at one joint. I also asked the section officer and he said the feeder is lightly loaded now because we had shifted load to a new feeder, which is exactly why it was not tripping. We went ahead with the maintenance and when the joint was opened it was badly oxidised. The report was correct and completely misleading at the same time.
Q3_text: For SCADA points I know that if a value is not changing at all then the point is dead. A live current value always moves a little. That is the simplest check and I have taught it to my engineers also. Our system does flag a communication failure for the remote terminal unit, that much is available. What it does not flag is a sensor which is sending a wrong but steady value, and that is the more dangerous case, because everybody believes a green screen.
Q4_text: Yes, our energy audit report was showing losses in one division coming down sharply, from about 19 per cent to 11, and nobody could explain what we had done to achieve it. I did not believe it because no new metering had been done in that area. On checking, the feeder meter reading was being estimated for two months because the meter modem was faulty, and the estimation was based on the previous year, so the whole loss figure was calculated on an assumed number.
Q5_text: I sent it in writing to the metering wing and marked a copy to the director. Because the loss figure goes to the regulator, this became serious immediately and there is a proper record of it. The meter was replaced in about three weeks and the figures for those two months were revised and reported as revised. In our sector if you do not correct such a thing and it is found later, it becomes a compliance issue, so people do act.
Q6_text: The written record carries the weight. In our system if you have raised a point in the log book or on the file, then even five years later it stands by you. A report is respected but everybody knows that a report is prepared by somebody, so the question is always who verified it. I would say the personal judgement of a senior engineer is still respected here, more than in other industries, because when something fails they need the man who understands the equipment.
Q7_text: In safety related matters they are not equal, and the imbalance is in favour of caution. If I stop a line for maintenance and it turns out nothing was wrong, at worst I have spent some money and lost some hours. If I go by the report, keep the line running and there is a failure, especially if somebody is injured, then there is an enquiry and my signature is on the deferment note. We are trained to take the safe side and nobody will question you for being cautious.
Q8_text: Our junior engineer at a substation kept reporting that the battery bank voltage was showing normal on the panel while the actual reading with a multimeter was low. He put it in the daily log every day for about ten days. Because it was in the log, when the shift in charge did the weekly review it got picked up and the charger was found faulty. That is exactly the benefit of the log book, it is old fashioned but it works.
Q9_text: It does narrow it. When we review reliability the discussion is about tripping counts and duration, so the actions become feeder shifting, tree cutting and transformer augmentation. Options like changing the maintenance philosophy from time based to condition based, or training the local staff properly, do not appear because the dashboard cannot show them. Those are the ones which would give a permanent improvement.

Q1_text:
Four regularly:
- an engineering delivery dashboard, cycle time and deployment frequency
- a service health board, error rates and latency
- a product analytics dashboard for the funnels my teams own
- a hiring and attrition view, weekly

The interesting part is that the dashboard was not wrong, it was answering a question nobody had asked.

Q1_text: A sales and margin dashboard in Power BI which refreshes at 6 am, a stock cover report, and a markdown tracker during end of season sale. First thing I look at is the refresh timestamp in the corner, genuinely, because I have been burnt by presenting stale numbers in a morning call. The dashboard showed sell through at 46 per cent for one style group which put it in the deeper markdown bucket automatically. What I noticed was that about 30 per cent of the stock of those styles was sitting in two warehouses and had never reached the stores, so it could not have sold, and including it in the denominator made the sell through look far worse than the actual store performance. I pulled the store level stock and reran the sell through on stock actually available at store. It came to around 61 per cent. We took a shallower markdown on those styles and saved a reasonable amount of margin. It took me most of a day to establish that, and the automatic recommendation would have taken thirty seconds.
Q3_text: Partly I can tell, because our BI team put a last refreshed stamp on the main dashboards and it turns red if the refresh failed. That covers the daily sales feed.
